turns.prompt_text: I have a sieve that I defat fried some food in But now it is very dirty I have tried boiling it, soaking it in lemon juice I wonder what else I could do Attached 1 file. - 102c7594-ded7-4ac5-a2f8-32e7c1d4e39b
turns.response_html:
Deep-frying leaves behind polymerized fat (oil that has basically turned into a tough, plastic-like varnish) and trapped carbonized food particles. Because this gunk is hydrophobic and chemically bonded, plain boiling water or mild acids like lemon juice won't quite cut through it.

To dissolve polymerized oil, you need to go high-alkaline or use mechanical agitation that can penetrate the fine mesh. Here are the most effective ways to clean it:

1. The High-Alkaline Boil (OxiClean or Baking Soda)

Since you are already set up to boil it, shifting the chemistry of the water will yield much better results.

  • The Method: Fill your pot with water, bring it to a simmer, and add 2–3 tablespoons of baking soda or 1 scoop of OxiClean (sodium percarbonate).
  • How it works: This creates a highly alkaline environment that attacks and breaks down the fatty acid chains. Let the sieve simmer in it for 15–20 minutes. The baked-on grease should soften into a wipeable sludge.

2. Heavy-Duty Degreaser or Oven Cleaner

If the oil is severely polymerized, household detergents won't touch it, but a dedicated solvent will.

  • The Method: Spray the sieve generously with a heavy-duty kitchen degreaser (like Dawn Powerwash or Krud Kutter) or standard yellow-cap oven cleaner (Easy-Off). Let it sit in a plastic bag or your sink for 30 minutes to an hour.
  • Safety Note: If using oven cleaner, do this in a well-ventilated area and wear gloves. Rinse thoroughly and scrub with dish soap afterward.

3. Mechanical Extraction (The Toothbrush Trick)

Mesh acts like a thousands-of-tiny-windows trap. Wiping it with a sponge just glides over the surface without penetrating the holes.

  • The Method: After soaking or boiling the sieve using one of the methods above, take an old, stiff-bristled toothbrush or a stiff dish brush.
  • The Technique: Instead of scrubbing side-to-side (which just jams the gunk further into the mesh corners), poke and dab the bristles straight down through the grid. This physically punches the softened debris out of the micro-holes.

4. Pressure or Force

If you have a kitchen sink faucet with a high-pressure "spray" or "shield" mode, blast the hot water through the reverse side of the mesh after it has soaked in a degreaser. The reverse pressure will pop the lodged particles right out.

turns.prompt_text: So using high alkalinity can clean it. Can I mix baking soda and boiling the water or is that a bad idea? What about baking soda and lemon juice? What would happen if I used isopropyl alcohol? I imagine that's not ideal here. That's more for disinfectant What about some SOS? I would really prefer and I'm perfectly okay with letting this soak overnight for a day or a more in order to get it cleaned. I'm not in a time crunch I'm willing to use whatever, but if it's somewhat toxic or dangerous with fumes or whatever, let me know and I'll put it outside. But as long as it gets it pristine and clean
turns.response_html:
Here is the breakdown of how those options work, what is safe to combine, and how to set up an effortless overnight soak to get that mesh pristine.

The Chemistry: What Works and What Fails

1. Baking Soda + Boiling Water (Excellent Idea)

Yes, do this. This is actually the ideal way to use baking soda for heavy grease. When you heat sodium bicarbonate (baking soda) in boiling water, it undergoes a chemical transformation called thermal decomposition, turning into sodium carbonate (washing soda).

  • Sodium carbonate has a much higher pH (around 11) than regular baking soda (around 8).
  • This highly alkaline environment turns the hardened, polymerized oils into a water-soluble soap (a process called saponification).

2. Baking Soda + Lemon Juice (Bad Idea / Cancels Out)

Avoid this. Mixing them creates a satisfying fizz, but chemically, you are just neutralizing your cleaning power.

  • Lemon juice is an acid (low pH) and baking soda is a base (high pH).
  • When mixed, they react to form carbon dioxide gas (the bubbles), water, and a neutral salt. You end up with a weak, neutral solution that won't cut through polymerized oil at all.

3. Isopropyl Alcohol (IPA)

Ineffective here. You are exactly right—it is great for disinfecting and stripping light, wet oils (like finger oils on electronics), but it cannot dissolve polymerized or baked-on cooking fat. Once oil has been heated and bonded into that plastic-like layer, alcohol won't touch it.

4. S.O.S Pads (Steel Wool + Soap)

Highly effective, but use with care. S.O.S pads are loaded with a heavy-duty degreasing soap and the steel wool provides great mechanical abrasion.

  • The Catch: Because it’s a fine mesh sieve, heavy scrubbing with steel wool can occasionally fray or snag the tiny wires if you scrub too hard, or leave behind tiny fragments of steel wool that can rust later. If you use it, use a light hand or use it after a soak when the gunk is already loose.

The "Zero-Effort" Overnight Strategy (Outdoor Option)

Since you aren't in a time crunch and want it pristine without standing over a stove scrubbing, you can use a heavy-duty soak. Because you mentioned being open to stronger methods if they are placed outside, Oven Cleaner is your silver bullet. It contains sodium hydroxide (lye), which completely destroys polymerized fat.

The Pristine-Mesh Overnight Soak:

  1. Take it Outside: Take a large, heavy-duty Ziploc bag (or a trash bag) and your sieve outside.
  2. Spray Heavily: Spray the sieve generously with standard heavy-duty oven cleaner (like yellow-cap Easy-Off). Make sure the mesh is completely coated.
  3. Seal and Wait: Put the sieve in the bag, seal it tightly to lock in the moisture so it doesn't dry out, and leave it outside (on a porch or in a garage) overnight or for up to 24 hours. The fumes will be contained in the bag and kept away from your kitchen.
  4. The Rinse: The next day, wear kitchen gloves, take it out of the bag, and rinse it under hot water. The polymerized grease should literally melt off the mesh like jelly. Give it a quick wash with normal dish soap, and it will look brand new.

If you don't have oven cleaner on hand and want to stick to kitchen ingredients right now, go with the Baking Soda + Boiling Water method for 20 minutes—it will do a massive amount of the heavy lifting right away!

turns.prompt_text: For some reason I think about salt. Is salt something that would help here?
turns.response_html:
Salt can actually be incredibly helpful, but only as a mechanical scrubbing agent, not as a chemical dissolver.

If you pour salt onto a wet surface, it doesn't melt grease the way a strong alkaline cleaner does. Instead, it acts like a natural, food-safe sandpaper.

Here is why salt is a favorite in professional kitchens for cleaning tough grease, and how it applies to your sieve:

How Salt Helps (The "Scrubbing Paste" Method)

Because salt crystals are hard, sharp, and don't immediately dissolve in pure oil, they make an excellent abrasive that won't ruin metal.

  • The Technique: You would take the dry or slightly damp sieve, pour a generous amount of coarse salt (like Kosher salt or sea salt) directly onto the mesh, and add just a tiny drop of dish soap to create a thick, gritty paste.
  • The Action: Using a stiff brush or a cloth, you scrub the salt paste into the mesh. The sharp crystals physically shear and scrape away the hardened oil droplets trapped in the grid.

The Verdict for Your Sieve

While salt is legendary for cleaning cast iron skillets or flat-top grills, it has a slight drawback with a fine mesh sieve: the salt crystals are often larger than the micro-holes in the mesh. It will do a great job cleaning the surface faces of the wire, but it might not be able to get inside the tiny gaps to push the plugs of dirt out.

Summary: If you want to use salt, it works best as a finishing step after you have done the baking soda boil or oven-cleaner soak to physically scour away whatever loosened residue is still clinging to the wires!

turns.prompt_text: Doesn't matter whether there's iodine in salt
turns.response_html:
No, it doesn't matter at all for cleaning purposes!

The iodine in iodized salt is present in such microscopic amounts (usually around 45 parts per million of potassium iodate) that it won't change the chemical or physical behavior of the salt when you are scrubbing with it.

The only things that matter when using salt as a cleaning abrasive are:

  • The crystal size: Coarser salts (like Kosher salt or sea salt) have larger, sharper edges which make them better "sandpaper" for scraping off grime. Standard table salt (which is usually what has iodine added) has much smaller crystals, but it will still work fine if you pack it into a thick paste with a little dish soap.
  • Solubility: Keep the water to an absolute minimum while scrubbing so the crystals don't dissolve before they can do their mechanical work.

So feel free to use whatever cheap table salt or iodized salt you have in the pantry—it will do the job just fine!

turns.prompt_text: So salt is really useful as an abrasive but I don't think there's any chemical properties that help
turns.response_html:
You are exactly right. Chemically speaking, salt ($\text{NaCl}$) is completely neutral ($\text{pH} \approx 7$) and stable, so it won’t break down or dissolve the fat molecules at all.

Its usefulness is 100% mechanical. The sharp edges of the sodium chloride crystals act like a microscopic scraper to slice through the hardened, plastic-like layer of polymerized oil.

Since you have time on your side and want it pristine, your best bet is a two-step approach that combines both chemistry and mechanics:

  1. The Chemical Attack: Use the high-alkaline baking soda boil (which converts it to washing soda with a high $\text{pH}$) or the overnight oven cleaner soak. This chemically breaks the bonds of the polymerized oil and turns it into a soft, jelly-like sludge.
  2. The Mechanical Finish: Once the gunk is soft, hit it with that salt paste, an S.O.S pad, or a stiff toothbrush to easily punch the loosened residue right out of the mesh holes.

Good luck getting it back to brand new! Which method are you leaning toward starting with?
